What the name encodes

The platform is named for what it does, and each part of the name corresponds to a concrete architectural commitment rather than a slogan.

NameReads asWhat it means in the codebase
ATRIAArtifact Transformation Raw DICOM / NIfTI / AVI becomes a PNG-plus-JSON corpus, then classification sets, then a LoRA adapter, then revision bundles. Every stage is a typed transformation of an artifact into another artifact, and each one is reproducible from the last.
Resource Interoperability One contract — frames/ + tracings.json + metadata.csv — is read and written by every stage. It is why a clinician's correction can re-enter training with no conversion step, and why coordinates are normalised to [0, 1000] so any frame resolution interoperates with any other.
in Artificial Intelligence MedGemma 1.5 4B, adapted with QLoRA across the language and vision towers — the open-weight layer that makes the transformation learnable rather than hand-engineered.
EchoTraceTracing the echocardiographic frame The task itself: the left-ventricular endocardial border, emitted as an ordered sequence of points a human can inspect, edit and hand back.

The interoperability commitment is the one that shapes everything else. Because the corpus contract is symmetric — the same three artifacts in and out — the human-in-the-loop cycle is a property of the data model, not a feature bolted on afterwards.

1 · Why coordinates instead of a mask

Tracing the endocardial border is the most repeated manual act in echocardiography. Every ejection fraction and every volume measurement begins with a clinician drawing a line around a moving, noisy, partly-visible chamber.

The standard machine-learning answer is semantic segmentation: predict a mask. For a clinical workflow that answer has a specific, practical weakness — a mask is hard to correct. A cardiologist who disagrees with one section of a boundary cannot nudge it; they can only repaint it. And the disagreement is discarded, because there is no compact structure recording "the model said here, the human said there."

Reframing the output as an ordered list of boundary coordinates changes what the system can do:

[{"polygon_2d": [[184, 496], [205, 490], [225, 486], ...],
  "label": "left_ventricle_endocardium"}]

Coordinates are normalised to a [0, 1000] grid, so the contract is resolution-independent — a 112×112 EchoNet frame and an 843×512 CAMUS frame share one output space, and no upload is ever resized.

That single change buys three things a mask does not:

  • Editable output. Vertices are draggable. Correction is a gesture, not a repaint.
  • A diffable record. Model polygon and human polygon are the same data type, so disagreement is measurable per point.
  • A training signal. The corrected polygon is a label in the original training format — corrections flow back with no conversion step.
Why a VLM is the right tool here. A segmentation network has no mechanism to emit JSON. A general vision-language model does but lacks medical grounding. MedGemma provides both — and being open-weight, it can be adapted where the data already lives.

median point-to-curve  4.98 mm
Dice vs training polygon  0.836
Note the prose. The model narrates before it answers, and wraps the payload in a fenced block with a label field. Nothing downstream assumes otherwise: the parser extracts the fence, validates the schema, checks bounds and tests for self-intersection, and fails loudly rather than silently repairing a malformed generation. Across the 200 held-out frames this succeeded 200 times out of 200. All 200 raw responses ship in the benchmark data.

What the adapter actually does

On 200 held-out frames from 50 patients it had never seen, the fine-tuned model returned a valid, in-bounds, editable polygon every single time. Not 199 of 200. Every frame parsed, every coordinate landed inside the image, and 178 of the 200 contours came back within one point of the target density. A 4-billion-parameter open-weight model, adapted in 128 minutes on one GPU, writing geometry a cardiologist can pick up and edit.

A note on how to read the accuracy numbers. Later sections report Dice alongside our primary metric, because the segmentation literature reports Dice and comparison is useful. But this is not a segmentation network, and reading 0.744 against a purpose-built U-Net is a category error. A U-Net emits pixels; it has no mechanism for emitting a structure a human can edit, and no way to record a correction. The question here was whether a general-purpose vision-language model could produce clinically usable geometry as text, reliably enough to put in front of a clinician. That question now has an answer, with the error quantified frame by frame rather than asserted.

The two templates are identical but for one clause. The training variant tells the model which acquisition window and which point in the cardiac cycle it is looking at; the generic variant does not. Every number published here was measured with the training-matched prompt: the same string the fine-tuning saw. Serving a fine-tuned adapter a prompt it was not trained on is a silent distribution shift, and it is the easiest way to make a working adapter look broken.

What the contract does not specify: how many points. There is no “30” anywhere in the prompt, and no count constraint of any kind. Thirty is a property of the training targets: the reference preprocessors resample each expert contour to 30 index-uniform points. The model is free to emit any number, and does: across the 200 held-out frames it produced 29 to 53 points, exactly 30 on 80 frames and 30 or 31 on 178. Nothing downstream assumes a count, a winding direction, or an explicitly closed ring, because CAMUS and EchoNet disagree on all three.

Both templates ship verbatim in src/atria_echotrace/ml/prompts.py, transcribed from the notebook cells that produced the adapters, with the source line numbers recorded in the module docstring.

4 · End-to-end pipeline

Every stage is independently enterable from a CLI (ingest, classify, train, evaluate, export-corpus, publish-adapter) or from the browser workstation. The loop at the bottom is the point: the clinician's correction becomes the next generation's ground truth, in the same format training already consumes.

The preprocessing scripts are vendored byte-identically and re-run to reproduce the training corpus exactly — 22,048 frames / 11,024 cases. Provenance is executable, not asserted.

Three ways in — the same pipeline

Nothing above is a bespoke script. The pipeline is enterable at whichever level suits you, and each entry point produces artifacts the next stage consumes unchanged.

5 · The QLoRA configuration

Read directly from adapter_config.json and training_args.bin (a trl.SFTConfig, 134 fields) in the released checkpoints — not from notebook defaults.

Both published adapters share one recipe. Of 134 SFTConfig fields, exactly two differ — output_dir and logging_dir. One configuration, two datasets an order of magnitude apart in size, both converging without retuning.

LoRA

FieldValueFieldValue
r32biasnone
lora_alpha32use_rslora / use_dorafalse / false
lora_dropout0.05task_typeCAUSAL_LM
modules_to_savelm_head, embed_tokens

target_modules — 10 modules, and this is the interesting part

q_proj  k_proj  v_proj  o_proj      <- attention projections
gate_proj  up_proj  down_proj       <- language-tower MLP
fc1  fc2  out_proj                  <- SigLIP VISION-tower MLP + attention output

fc1, fc2 and out_proj are vision-encoder modules. Adapting the visual tower — not just the language head — is what lets the model learn what an endocardial border looks like rather than only how to format an answer. It is also precisely what the failure in §8 silently switched off.

6.1 The recipe was found, not guessed

Three runs share the identical CAMUS training split, so they isolate one variable. Learning rate 1e-5 never leaves the plateau: the model is still underfitting when the schedule ends. 2e-4 over eight epochs learns, but stalls at 0.390. 1e-4 over five epochs reaches 0.259: a better result in 125 steps than eight epochs achieved in 376, and in well under half the elapsed time.

6.2 The recipe transferred without retuning

Run 6 and Run 5 differ only in the data they were shown. Of the 134 fields in the serialised SFTConfig, exactly two differ: the output and logging directories. One is a 1,600-frame corpus finishing in 125 optimizer steps; the other is 16,576 frames over 1,295 steps, an order of magnitude larger. Both converge, and both finish at their minimum eval loss.

37 of 38 fields identical. The one that differs is highlighted: a version stamp, not a hyperparameter. The full SFTConfig tells the same story: 132 of 134 fields match, and the two that do not are the output and logging paths.
This is the transferability claim, and it is falsifiable. If the recipe only worked on the corpus it was tuned against, the larger run would have needed its own learning rate, schedule or batch size. It did not. For a developer with their own echocardiography archive, that is the difference between adopting a pipeline and restarting a search.

6.3 What it actually costs

The shipped CAMUS adapter took 128 minutes of training on a single GPU. The larger EchoNet adapter took 21.3 hours. Throughput roughly doubled between the early runs and the final two — 0.66 to ~1.06 samples/second: when the per-device batch went from 2 to 4.

That matters more than it looks. A centre wanting to fit this to their own labelling conventions is not committing to a cluster or a multi-week programme; on a CAMUS-sized corpus they are committing to an afternoon. The five runs that logged a runtime total 36 hours between them: the entire search, dead ends included, on one GPU.

7 · Evaluation — the gallery is the primary evidence

Test set: the official CAMUS subgroup_testing split — 50 patients, 200 frames, selected by the dataset authors' own split file and never seen in training. Quality mix: 94 Good · 76 Medium · 30 Poor. Inference: 4-bit NF4 + double-quant, bf16 compute, training-matched prompt.

Three frames that carry the argument

Look closely at the worst case. It is the most informative image in the set. The prediction is a well-formed ventricle traced in the wrong place — correct point count, no self-intersection, displaced by roughly a chamber width. The model did not produce noise; it confidently traced the wrong structure. No scalar metric expresses that, and it is exactly the failure a reviewing clinician must catch. This is the argument for human-in-the-loop, made visually.

The full range — 24 frames sampled evenly by rank

Ranked best to worst across all 200 held-out frames, every ninth frame. This is the honest shape of the model's behaviour: tight agreement at the top, gradual drift through the middle, and a small number of gross mislocalisations at the end.

Each caption gives the frame's median point-to-curve distance, its acquisition quality, view and cardiac instant, and its rank among the 200. All 200 rendered frames, the per-frame CSVs and the raw model responses ship in the repository.

7.2 Primary metric — point-to-curve distance

The primary question for a coordinate-generating model is "do the predicted points land on the expert tracing?" That is point-to-curve distance: the shortest Euclidean distance from each predicted point to the expert polyline (piecewise-linear, edge projection with the parameter clipped to [0,1]) — not distance to the nearest vertex, and not rasterised mask-boundary distance.

Accuracy degrades monotonically with acquisition quality — 4.61 → 6.40 → 6.79 mm. That is the behaviour a clinician expects from a system genuinely reading the image, and it is stronger evidence of a sane model than any single headline number.

7.4 The representation is not the bottleneck

Before attributing error to the model we measured the discretisation ceiling — how much accuracy is lost purely by representing an expert mask as 30 index-uniform points. This is reference-versus-reference and costs no inference:

Ceiling (200 frames)DiceMADHD95
30-point representation vs expert mask 0.99050.214 mm0.542 mm

The 30-point representation is near-lossless. A Dice of 0.744 is therefore a property of the model, not of the output format — and there is substantial headroom before the representation constrains anything.

Why we do not lead with Dice 0.8924. That figure — and 0.7026 for EchoNet — are n = 1 smoke values printed by a regression test, and the CAMUS one is a 4-chamber frame, the best-performing view. They are observations, not accuracy. The defensible figures are the n = 200 numbers above. More fundamentally, region overlap measures a downstream construction: the adapter emits coordinates, and converting them to a mask inserts a rasterisation step the model never performed.

7.5 View, image quality, and a confound worth naming

The 200 frames split evenly by view — 100 four-chamber, 100 two-chamber, and CAMUS grades image quality per acquisition window, not per patient. In this test set 16 of 50 patients (32%) carry a different grade for their 2CH and 4CH studies, so the two axes can be crossed honestly.

Median point-to-curveGoodMedium Poorall
4-chamber 4.53 n=56 6.27 n=34 6.60 n=10 4.76 n=100
2-chamber 4.81 n=38 6.46 n=42 7.00 n=20 5.45 n=100
all4.61 n=94 6.40 n=76 6.79 n=30 4.98 n=200

Acquisition quality costs the same in both windows. Good → Poor is +2.07 mm in 4CH and +2.19 mm in 2CH — +45.6% in each. View difficulty and image quality act independently; there is no interaction between them. That is a statement about the imaging, not the model, and it is actionable: a lab that improves its acquisition recovers roughly a third of the error, whichever window it is working in.

And a correction to our own earlier claim. We have reported that “two-chamber views are weaker” — 5.45 against 4.76 mm. The cross-tab shows most of that is a quality-mix confound: 2CH carries twice the Poor frames (20 vs 10) and far fewer Good (38 vs 56). Standardising both views onto the pooled quality mix:

crude gap +0.70 mm  →  quality-adjusted gap +0.26 mm.

62% of the apparent view gap is the imaging, not the view. The genuine view effect is small and consistent within every stratum (+0.28 / +0.19 / +0.40 mm). The model is more view-robust than our own headline number suggested, and the thing worth targeting with further training is Poor-quality frames in both views, not two-chamber imaging.

Computed from data/pointwise.csv joined to the per-view ImageQuality field of each patient's CAMUS Info_*.cfg. Poor is n = 30 across both views, enough to state a direction and not a coefficient.

8 · A PEFT failure mode that never raises

This was found, repaired, and is guarded by a regression test. Every number on this page comes from the repaired adapter. It is written up because the failure is generic: it belongs to how PEFT resolves module paths across a library upgrade, not to MedGemma, to Gemma 3, or to this project. If you have fine-tuned a vision tower and upgraded transformers since, it is worth ten seconds of your time.

The published adapters were trained when Gemma 3 nested the vision encoder as vision_tower.vision_model.encoder. Transformers 5.x flattened that path to vision_tower.encoder.

Consequence: 324 of the checkpoint's 802 tensors addressed a module path that no longer existed. PEFT emits a non-fatal warning and continues. Every vision-tower lora_B therefore stayed at its zero initialisation — and a LoRA update of B·A with B = 0 contributes exactly nothing.

The model loaded. It ran. It produced plausible contours. Roughly 40 % of the fine-tuning was inert, and the only signal was a warning in a log most pipelines filter out.

If you fine-tune a vision tower and later upgrade transformers, check for this:

status = engine.status()["adapter_load"]
assert status["fully_loaded"], status
# -> remapped / vision_lora_b_active / vision_lora_b

The fix is a key remap at load time, guarded by a regression test that fails if it ever silently returns. Do not trust "the adapter loaded." Verify that every tensor found a home — and never filter warnings out of a fine-tuning log.

9 · What it does and does not do

  • Scope: left ventricle only. The published adapters were tuned on LV; the left atrium is out of distribution.
  • Structural validity: 25 / 200 (12.5 %) of generated polygons self-intersect — a downstream area calculation would silently mishandle these.
  • Point count: median 31, range 29–53. Only 40 % emit exactly 30; 89 % (178/200) land on 30 or 31. The count is not hard-constrained by decoding.
  • View gap: 2-chamber is consistently weaker than 4-chamber (5.45 vs 4.76 mm; Dice 0.723 vs 0.765).
  • Failure mode: the worst cases are plausible shapes in the wrong location, not obvious garbage — which is precisely why review is mandatory.
  • Latency: median 86 s/frame on a pre-Ampere Quadro RTX 5000 (sm_75, no native bf16). Not a real-time system on that hardware.
  • Scale: 200 frames on CAMUS. The full 2,752-frame combined split has not been run, and no EchoNet benchmark of equivalent rigour exists yet.
  • EchoNet ED/ES labels are transposed in 99 % of cases — a property of the source data. We flag and deliberately do not correct it, because relabelling at inference would push every request outside the adapter's training distribution.
  • Training reproduction: the shipped training command ports the notebook recipe, which differs from the published adapters' configuration in §3.

Three transferable lessons, independent of cardiology

  1. Match the metric to the output. We first scored a coordinate generator with Dice and ejection fraction. Both measured downstream constructions. Re-scoring with point-to-curve changed the interpretation, not the model.
  2. Render your predictions. The 12.5 % self-intersection rate and the confidently-misplaced worst case were both found by looking, not by aggregating.
  3. A partially-loaded adapter is indistinguishable from a working one at the output level. Assert completeness.

11 · Make your own adapter

There are two ways to take this further, for two different people. They are not two doors to the same room.

Track A · understand and modify

The research notebook

For someone who wants to change the method: the prompt, the target representation, the LoRA placement.

  1. Read it on GitHub. 38 cells, 30 of them code, with stored outputs, so you can follow what happened without executing anything.
  2. Open it in Colab. It runs without gated weights, so you can trace the full flow before requesting adapter access.
  3. Change one thing. The prompt template, the 30-point resampling, the target modules: each is a single cell.
  4. Re-run. On CAMUS, a full fine-tune is ~2 hours on one GPU.

Open in Colab →   View on GitHub

Track B · run it on your data

The CLI and the workstation

For someone who wants an adapter for their archive, with their labelling conventions, behind their own firewall.

  1. Bring your frames into the contract. 
    atria --dataset-dir <dir> ingest
  2. Inspect before you train. 
    atria --dataset-dir <dir> classify
  3. Fine-tune. 
    atria --dataset-dir <dir> train --output-dir ./my-adapter
  4. Benchmark, then close the loop. 
    atria --dataset-dir <dir> evaluate --adapter ./my-adapter
atria --dataset-dir <dir> serve
atria --dataset-dir <dir> export-corpus

Both tracks consume the same three-artifact contract and produce the same kind of adapter. The notebook is the origin of the recipe; the CLI is that recipe made operable. Neither requires the other.

Everything above is reproducible on your own data. The pipeline does not assume CAMUS or EchoNet: it assumes the three-artifact contract: frames, a tracings JSON, and a metadata CSV. Conform to that and every downstream stage works unchanged.

  1. Bring your frames into the corpus contract

    Point the ingest stage at your source. The vendored preprocessors are the reference implementation: they reproduce the published corpus byte-identically, so they are a working template for a new source rather than pseudocode.

    atria --dataset-dir /path/to/your/data ingest
  2. Check what you have before you train

    Derive classification sets and inspect the split. This is where labelling problems surface: it is the stage that exposed the per-view quality grading in CAMUS and the transposed end-diastole/end-systole labels in EchoNet.

    atria --dataset-dir /path/to/your/data classify
  3. Fine-tune

    The published recipe is the default: QLoRA rank 32, 4-bit NF4, bf16, effective batch 64, 5 epochs, linear 1e-4 with 3% warmup. On a 1,600-frame corpus this is the 128-minute run in the table above.

    atria --dataset-dir /path/to/your/data train --output-dir ./my-adapter
  4. Benchmark it against your own held-out split

    The harness writes per-frame JSONL as it goes, so an interrupt costs one frame, and it renders every prediction for visual review. Report point-to-curve distance, not only Dice: the metric has to match the representation.

    atria --dataset-dir /path/to/your/data evaluate --adapter ./my-adapter
  5. Close the loop

    Serve the adapter in the workstation, let a clinician correct vertices, and export the revisions back into the same corpus format. Their corrections become the next training set, which is the entire point of emitting coordinates instead of a mask.

    atria --dataset-dir /path/to/your/data export-corpus
One honest caveat on reproduction. atria train ports the notebook recipe; it is not a byte-exact replay of the Colab runs that produced the published adapters, and we do not claim it reproduces those weights. It reproduces the method. If you need the exact published artifacts, take them from Hugging Face.

12 · Built in the open

Everything here is built on open datasets and open model weights, and released the same way. Alongside the parts that worked, the record below includes the runs that did not, a defect we introduced ourselves, and the numbers we decided not to headline.

The runs that did not workRun 2 (lr 1e-5, never left the plateau) and Run 3 (lr 2e-4 over eight epochs, stalled at 0.390) ship with their full logs and plots, so the search is visible and not only its result.
A defect that invalidated our own work324 of 802 adapter tensors were loading into nothing. We found it ourselves, published it, and turned it into a regression test rather than quietly re-running.
12.5%of generated polygons self-intersect. Nobody asked. It appears in the limitations, the ladder and the per-frame CSV.
n = 1A Dice of 0.8924 exists in our own test output. It is a single four-chamber frame, so we refuse to headline it, and say so explicitly rather than letting it circulate.
The metric we got wrong firstWe scored a coordinate model with Dice and ejection fraction before realising both measure a downstream construction. The wrong turn is documented, not erased.
Every raw model responseAll 200 verbatim generations, prose preambles included, in the benchmark data, so anyone can check the parser against the actual text.

Why this is a platform and not a demo

The adapters were trained on open datasets — CAMUS and EchoNet-Dynamic, each acquired under its own licence: on top of open weights, MedGemma 1.5 4B. The preprocessing scripts that built the corpus are in the repository, vendored byte-identically so they reproduce that corpus rather than approximate it. The checkpoints, including the optimiser state, go to Hugging Face.

Which means the work is resumable, not just readable. Neither shipped run is converged: both were stopped while training and evaluation loss were still falling, to fix a reference point rather than to chase a number. Anyone can pick up the same recipe and keep going: on the same open corpora, or on their own archive, behind their own firewall, against their own labelling conventions — a specific view, a specific chamber, a specific population.

Open datasets, open weights, open preprocessing, open benchmark. The substrate is published rather than the product, so that clinicians who know where the contours are wrong and developers who can build a better adapter both have something to work from. The stage is yours. The Adimension · bridging human ingenuity and machine intelligence

13 · Built on the DEITY Principles

ATRIA EchoTrace is the reference implementation of the DEITY Principles Framework (Anwer, Eur Heart J Imaging Methods Pract). Each principle forced a decision you can check in the code:

  • Data — original preprocessors vendored byte-identically; the corpus is reproduced, not described.
  • Ethics — known data defects surfaced, never silently repaired. Physical areas in cm² are withheld when pixel spacing is unknown rather than computed from a placeholder.
  • Informatics — the output is structure a human can read, diff and edit.
  • Technology — 4-bit, single GPU, offline-capable, local-first weights.
  • You — the clinician's correction is the product, and it re-enters training by design.
Intended use. ATRIA EchoTrace is research software. It is not a cleared or approved medical device and must not be used for diagnosis or direct patient care. Every contour is a proposal requiring independent review by a qualified echocardiographer. Human-in-the-loop review is architectural, not advisory — the interface exists to be corrected.
